data.title: Congenital melanocytic nevus — viva
data.summary: Nevi & hamartomas · 10 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Congenital melanocytic nevus** (Nevi & hamartomas)_

**Q1. Define congenital melanocytic naevus (CMN).**
- Benign melanocytic proliferation present at birth or appearing within the first 6 months ('tardive' up to 2 years); ~1% of newborns; NRAS mutations (Q61) in most large CMN, BRAF in small

**Q2. Classify by projected adult size.**
- Small <1.5 cm, medium 1.5–20 cm (M1 1.5–10, M2 >10–20), large 20–40 cm, giant >40 cm (projected adult size — head ×1.7, trunk/limbs ×3 growth from infancy)
- Satellite naevi counted (≤20, 20–50, >50) — more satellites → higher risk of neurocutaneous melanosis

**Q3. Clinical features.**
- Brown to black, often raised, mammillated or verrucous surface, hypertrichosis, may have nodules (proliferative nodules — usually benign), variegated colour; large CMN in 'bathing trunk' or 'garment' distribution with satellites
- Large/giant CMN may cause pruritus, xerosis, erosions; colour may lighten with time

**Q4. Risks associated with large CMN.**
- Melanoma: lifetime ~2–5% for large/giant (higher in giant >40 cm with many satellites); can arise in deep dermis/subcutis or CNS, often in first 5 years; small/medium — <1% lifetime, mainly after puberty at the dermo-epidermal junction
- Neurocutaneous melanosis: melanocytes in leptomeninges — hydrocephalus, seizures, developmental delay, CNS melanoma; screen with MRI brain and spine (ideally before 6 months of age) in large CMN or >20 satellite naevi

**Q5. Histopathology.**
- Naevus cells extending deep into reticular dermis and subcutis, around/within adnexa (hair follicles, eccrine ducts), nerves and vessels, splaying between collagen bundles in single-file arrangement — distinguishes from acquired naevi

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- Café-au-lait macule, Becker's naevus, nevus spilus, epidermal naevus, Mongolian spot, plexiform neurofibroma, smooth muscle hamartoma, mastocytoma, nevus sebaceous

**Q7. Management.**
- Individualised: clinical photographs and regular examination (palpation for nodules), dermoscopy; biopsy any new nodule, ulcer or rapid change
- Small/medium: observation or elective excision for cosmetic reasons or difficult-to-monitor sites (scalp)
- Large/giant: staged excision with tissue expanders, flaps, grafts (does not eliminate melanoma risk completely); curettage in neonatal period, dermabrasion, lasers (cosmetic; may hamper monitoring)
- MRI CNS screening as above; psychosocial support; trametinib (MEK inhibitor) under study

**Q8. What is neurocutaneous melanosis?**
- Proliferation of melanocytes in leptomeninges/brain parenchyma with large/giant CMN (especially posterior axial location with multiple satellite naevi >20) — hydrocephalus, seizures, developmental delay, leptomeningeal melanoma; MRI brain with contrast in the first 6 months of life (before myelination masks it)

**Q9. What is the molecular basis?**
- Post-zygotic NRAS (Q61) mutations in ~70–80% of large CMN; BRAF in small/medium; explains multiple satellite naevi from a single clone

**Q10. What should prompt biopsy in CMN follow-up?**
- New nodule (proliferative nodules are common and usually benign but need histology), ulceration, rapid colour/size change, pain, bleeding; melanoma in large CMN often arises deep (dermal/subcutaneous) in the first 5 years

## Quick spotter facts
- Large hairy pigmented naevus with satellites — giant CMN; MRI for neurocutaneous melanosis
- Projected adult size >20 cm = large

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Congenital melanocytic naevi). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
